title: 24 Indian Seafarers Safe After Tankers Hit in Hormuz and Off Romania, Minister Says
excerpt: Crude tanker MT ST 3, with 15 Indian crew, was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on October 16; chemical tanker Yara J, with nine Indians aboard, was hit by a drone at Sulina Anchorage on October 14. No casualties on either vessel.
body:
• All 24 Indian seafarers aboard two tankers struck in separate incidents this week are safe, with no casualties or injuries, Union shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal said on Friday.
  • MT ST 3, a crude oil tanker with 15 Indian crew, was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on October 16.
  • Chemical tanker Yara J, with nine Indian crew, was hit by a drone at Sulina Anchorage, Romania, on October 14; Reuters reported its crew unharmed and the ship towed to Constanta.
  • The attacks extend a pattern: on October 11 a drone hit MT Petro Dolphin at Sohar Anchorage, leaving two of its 11 Indian seafarers missing, and India has condemned the strikes and called for de-escalation.

Two vessels carrying a total of 24 Indian seafarers were struck in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and off Romania this week, Union shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal said on Friday, adding that every crew member was safe. The government is monitoring both situations and is in close contact with the ship management companies, according to The Times of India.

"All 24 Indian nationals across both vessels are completely safe with no casualties or injuries."

— Sarbananda Sonowal, Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways

Two incidents, two seas

The crude oil tanker MT ST 3, carrying 15 Indian seafarers, was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on October 16. Two days earlier, on October 14, the chemical tanker Yara J, carrying nine Indian seafarers, was hit by a drone at Sulina Anchorage in Romania. Reuters reported that Yara J, a Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker, was struck inside Romanian waters, its crew unharmed, and the vessel towed to the port of Constanta. It was one of two tankers hit by drones within about 12 hours near Romania's Black Sea coast; the other, the Wine Trader, lost seven sailors, for whom Romanian rescuers were still searching on Friday.

A pattern, not an episode

The Hormuz strike follows the Ministry of External Affairs' condemnation on October 11 of attacks on commercial vessels in the strait. In that incident, the tanker MT Petro Dolphin, carrying 11 Indian seafarers, was reportedly struck by a drone at Sohar Anchorage: nine crew were rescued and two remained missing. Another vessel, the Marshall Islands-flagged MT VALTHERA was hit by an unidentified projectile and caught fire, with all 11 Indian seafarers aboard reported safe. India reiterated that the safety of its seafarers is a priority and called for an end to attacks on commercial vessels and civilian infrastructure, and for freedom of navigation through international waterways.

The Black Sea front

India has raised the same concerns over Black Sea shipping, where the foreign ministry has condemned strikes on commercial vessels and called for an immediate cessation of violence. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has said India remains in contact with Russia and Ukraine over its proposal for safe shipping in the Black Sea and non-attack arrangements covering grain and energy exports. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two tankers near his coast were struck by drones, and a NATO military source attributed the drones to Russia — a spillover of the Ukraine war into lanes used by neutral merchant crews.

What happens next

For the families of the 24 crew members, the immediate news is the outcome every such alert hopes for: no one hurt. The structural question is unchanged — two of the world's most important energy corridors are now active conflict zones, and Indian nationals, who crew a significant share of the global merchant fleet, are exposed in both.
